title: Fed's September Meeting: Why a Rate Hike Is Back on the Table
description: Ahead of the Sept 15-16 FOMC meeting, expectations have shifted toward a possible rate hike amid energy-led inflation. Here's what that means for gold near $4,371.
bodyMarkdown:
Gold is trading around **$4,371 an ounce** on August 13, 2026, slipping roughly **1.2%** on the day as investors position for the Federal Reserve's next big decision. The central bank's September meeting has become the market's main focus — and, unusually for the past few years, the debate is no longer just about *when* rates will fall, but whether the Fed might actually **raise** them.

Here is what that shift means, why it is happening, and how it connects to the gold price.

## What the Fed has done so far in 2026

The Fed has been on hold for most of the year. At its **July meeting**, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) kept its benchmark federal funds rate in a target range of **3.50%–3.75%**, according to CNBC's recap of the decision. Notably, **three FOMC members dissented** — not because they wanted a cut, but because they wanted a hike. That is a meaningful signal: internal pressure is tilting hawkish (toward tighter policy), not dovish.

This continues a pattern from the June meeting, the first full gathering under new Fed Chair **Kevin Warsh**, when the committee also held at 3.50%–3.75% and described economic activity as expanding at a solid pace despite elevated uncertainty tied in part to conflict in the Middle East. The Fed has not cut rates since late 2025.

## Why September is the "first real test"

The story driving expectations is **energy-led inflation**. Oil prices have surged — topping **$100 a barrel** — amid supply-chain disruptions linked to the U.S.–Iran conflict, according to CBS News. When energy costs climb, they feed through to transport, manufacturing and food prices, making the Fed's 2% inflation target harder to reach.

That backdrop has changed the calculus among some forecasters. **J.P. Morgan Wealth Management** strategists now say they expect a **0.25-percentage-point rate hike at the September meeting**, a shift from their earlier base case of no rate changes in 2026. They cite two drivers: persistent supply shocks keeping energy costs elevated, and growing investor doubt about the Fed's willingness to keep inflation contained after it stood pat in July.

Chair Warsh has pledged to return inflation to 2% while offering markets few explicit clues about the path ahead — a deliberately non-committal stance that keeps expectations volatile.

## Key dates and what to watch

The next FOMC meeting is scheduled for **September 15–16**, with the rate decision released on the second day. Crucially, this meeting comes with a fresh **Summary of Economic Projections (SEP)** — the quarterly "dot plot" in which policymakers sketch their expectations for growth, inflation and the future path of rates. Because Warsh reportedly declined to submit individual projections at the June meeting, this SEP will be watched closely for a clearer read on where the committee stands.

Between now and then, the incoming inflation and jobs data will do the heavy lifting. Hotter inflation prints raise the odds of a hike; signs of a cooling labor market push in the other direction.

## How rate expectations move gold

Gold pays no interest and generates no dividends. That makes it especially sensitive to **interest rates and real yields** (the return on bonds after subtracting inflation). The relationship works like this:

- **Higher rates** raise the "opportunity cost" of holding gold, because cash and bonds become more attractive by comparison. That is typically a **headwind** for gold prices.
- **Lower rates** reduce that opportunity cost and tend to be **supportive** for gold.

So a growing chance of a September hike helps explain some of gold's softness this week. Yet the picture is not one-directional. Gold also behaves as an **inflation hedge** and a **safe-haven** asset during geopolitical stress. With energy-driven inflation running hot and a live Middle East conflict, those forces can cushion — or even offset — the drag from higher rates. That tug-of-war is a big reason gold remains near historically elevated levels even as the near-term rate outlook turns less friendly.

## The takeaway for everyday investors

The key point is that **expectations, not just decisions, move markets**. Gold prices react to the *probability* of the Fed's next move well before any announcement, so by the time September 16 arrives, much of the anticipated outcome may already be reflected in the price. The bigger market swings often come from **surprises** — a hike when markets expected a hold, or a dovish signal when they braced for tightening.

For a long-term holder, one meeting rarely changes the investment case. As several market strategists note, trying to time these moves is difficult; a steadier approach is to keep gold's role in a portfolio — diversification and a hedge against inflation and uncertainty — in view, rather than reacting to each data point. If your circumstances change, that is the moment to revisit your allocation.

**Bottom line:** heading into September 15–16, the market is weighing a genuine possibility of a rate *hike* driven by energy inflation and a hawkish-leaning FOMC. That has trimmed gold's shine in the short term, but the same inflation and geopolitical backdrop keeping the Fed cautious is also part of what keeps gold in demand.
